text: Private IP ranges like 192.168.0.0/16 aren't routable on the public internet. NAT is what lets many devices on a private network share one public IP — as traffic leaves, the router rewrites the source IP and tracks the port, so return traffic knows which internal device to go back to.

DHCP automates IP configuration with a four-step exchange remembered as DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The server hands out an address from a pool for a limited lease time. A rogue DHCP server — an unauthorized device answering with false information — is a real, documented attack technique.

DNS translates the names humans use into the IP addresses computers route by. A resolver walks a hierarchy of servers to find the authoritative answer, then caches it. DNS cache poisoning feeds a resolver a false answer to silently redirect victims, and DNS tunneling smuggles data inside DNS traffic to evade network controls.

These three services work together every time a device connects: DHCP configures it, DNS resolves the site name it wants to reach, and NAT rewrites the outbound traffic so the response can find its way back. Three separate services, one seamless experience when everything works — and three separate places something can quietly break.
